Background

Satellites, aircraft and mobile networks drown out the faint radio sky. Telescopes such as MeerKAT flag and discard the contaminated samples, a median 55% of every spectrogram in the data studied here. Every discarded sample is a hole in what the telescope measures.

Why it matters

21 cm cosmology searches for the faint signal of the early Universe in the delay spectrum. Gaps scatter bright foreground power across that spectrum, and flagging followed by averaging leaves fluctuations orders of magnitude larger than the signal itself (Offringa et al., 2019).

The same problem affects every radio telescope and grows as satellite constellations expand. The Square Kilometre Array, partly built in the South African Karoo, will face it at a larger scale.

Where the interference comes from

Aim and objectives

Can a conditional diffusion model reconstruct RFI-flagged MeerKAT data well enough to be preferable to discarding it, and under which conditions?

  1. Train without clean targets, on data that is itself corrupted.
  2. Test whether pre-training on simulation helps on real data.
  3. Measure what each design choice contributes.
  4. Find where reconstruction beats excision, and where it stops.
Methods

From the sky to repaired data

  1. 1. Receive

    MeerKAT’s dishes collect faint radio waves from the sky together with interference. This work uses one L-band observation, 900 to 1650 MHz.

  2. 2. Correlate

    Signals from every pair of dishes are combined into complex visibilities, one data stream per baseline.

  3. 3. Spectrogram

    Each baseline becomes a time and frequency image. Interference shows up as bright streaks.

  4. 4. Flag

    An automatic flagger removes the contaminated samples, a median 55% of each spectrogram in this data.

  5. 5. Fill with diffusion

    A conditional diffusion U-Net predicts amplitude and phase in the gaps from the surviving samples and the flag mask.

  6. 6. Write back

    Complete visibilities return to the measurement set, ready for any standard tool.

  7. 7. Science

    Delay spectra for 21 cm cosmology and continuum images are made from data without holes. The dashed line is the leakage gaps cause.

Data, model and evaluation

DataOne real MeerKAT L-band observation (900–1650 MHz, 1533 baselines) and Stimela2 simulations with synthetic RFI.
Pre-processDivide out the bandpass, encode phase as cos / sin, and tile at the native 512-channel resolution.
ModelA palette-style conditional diffusion U-Net (104.7 M parameters) that sees only the surviving samples and the flag mask.
TrainSupervised on simulation against noise-free truth, then self-supervised on real data by hiding samples that survived flagging.
Write backComplete complex visibilities go back into the measurement set, ready for any downstream tool.
EvaluateFake-hole tests in the delay spectrum against DPSS, GPR and excision, the protocol of Pagano et al., and WSClean images.

Simulation, where the truth is known

Simulated observations come with a noise-free true sky, so every fill can be scored exactly. They are used to pre-train the model and to test it before it sees real data.

A hard held-out simulated tile. 47% of it is hidden by interference and the fill correlates with the hidden truth at 0.75.

Results

Real MeerKAT data, before and after the AI fill

Six held-out examples from the real observation. Time runs left to right and frequency bottom to top. Drag across an image to compare the recording with the repair, or switch to side by side to see which samples were flagged.

faint bright flagged

Fill brightness is matched to neighbouring channels for display. Flagged percentages combine the telescope’s automatic flagger and an extra check for leftover interference.

Accuracy against other fillers

On 300 real held-out units whose test holes remove a median 43% of the signal power, the delay-spectrum error is 2.64× lower than DPSS in the foreground and 1.63× lower beyond 467 ns. It is better on 247 to 288 of the 300 units individually, and the result holds when resampled over antennas. It recovers 74–83% of the true high-delay power, against 62–67% for DPSS and 58–64% for excision.

The comparison uses three standard fillers and the default of doing nothing. DPSS interpolates with discrete prolate spheroidal sequences and is common in 21 cm analysis. GPR is Gaussian process regression. CLEAN deconvolves in the delay domain. Excision leaves the gaps empty.

Most accurate filler on an independent benchmark

Under the independent protocol of Pagano et al. (2023), on 400 real tiles, it has the lowest amplitude and phase error of every method, 27% below GPR on narrow holes and 35% below CLEAN on wide ones.

The win depends on gap width

The advantage shrinks as gaps widen. When the holes remove 81% of the power, DPSS wins by nearly 3×. Continuum images order the regimes the same way, 12.6× better than excision for single-channel gaps and unresolved by 32 channels.

Further findings

Divisive normalisation matters most (+9.6 dB). Without it the model learns to output a constant. Simulated pre-training more than halves the delay error.

Beyond 100 ns every method recovers, on average, less than a sixth of the true power. Neighbouring channels correlate at only 0.03, so the noise itself cannot be recovered, only its statistics.

On the real continuum image, filling did not improve the map (dynamic range 7159 to 6130), but it beat every other filler. DPSS lost three quarters of the dynamic range.

Conclusion

Use diffusion in-painting for delay-spectrum and 21 cm power-spectrum work when RFI gaps are narrow. Keep excision for continuum images and for wide contiguous bands. Good flagging still matters, since tight masks leave a more recoverable problem.

Limitations and next steps

Classical fills ran at default settings. The model works one baseline at a time and ignores array-wide coherence. Results cover a single MeerKAT L-band field. Next steps are array-level context, tuned classical baselines, and injection tests with signals of known strength.
